chunks: How chips talk to each other. The question: How do different chips talk to each other?
For two chips to exchange data, they must agree on four things. First, what voltages mean 1 and 0, so each chip can read the other. Second, when to read each bit.
Third, who a message is for, and where it starts. Fourth, what the bytes mean. I2C, SPI and UART are just different ways of settling the middle two.
The meaning part is usually a table of numbered registers.
Think of a phone call between two people. First they must hear each other clearly. Then they must talk at a pace both can follow.
They must also know who is calling whom, especially on a party line. Finally, they must speak a language both understand.
A bus fault is debugged the same way, one layer at a time.
Each box translates between layers.
Firmware sees a function call; the peripheral sees register writes and a state machine; the wire sees voltages; the sensor sees bits that select a register.
A failure in any box looks like "the sensor does not work", so debugging means checking each layer in turn.
Logic level: the voltage range that counts as a 1 or a 0 ("What logic levels are"). Common ground: both chips share the same 0 volts reference.
Clock: a tick that tells the receiver when each bit is valid, or the agreed bit speed if there is no clock wire.
Address: a number that picks which device on a shared bus should answer. Register: a numbered storage slot in a chip that holds a setting or a result.
Interrupt line: an extra wire a chip uses to say "something happened." A bus alone can't do that.
A microcontroller reads a temperature sensor at I2C address 0x48 ("0x" marks a number written in base 16, hexadecimal).
It sends that address, then the register number 0, then reads back two bytes: 0x0C and 0x80. Together they make 0x0C80, which is 12 times 256 plus 128 equals 3200 .
The datasheet (the maker's spec sheet) says each count is 1/128 degrees Celsius, so the temperature is 3200 over 128 equals 25. 0 degrees Celsius.
The wires carried only bytes; the datasheet gave them meaning. That is the whole idea.
"Chips talk by agreeing on four layers. Electrical: compatible logic levels and a shared ground.
Timing: either a shared clock like SPI and I2C, or an agreed baud rate with start bits like UART. Framing: a chip-select or an address to say who a message is for.
And meaning: usually a register map, so reading a sensor means writing a register address then reading bytes back.
I pick the bus by data rate, pin count, device count and distance."
